post.caption: Some pilgrim badges were tiny bells. The British Museum has one made in Canterbury around 1325 to 1350. Pilgrims pinned badges to hats and cloaks, to show where they had been. Many were cast from lead and tin, a mix called pewter. It melts at a low temperature, so badges were quick to make. Makers poured the hot metal into molds carved from stone. At the busiest shrines, around 100,000 badges may have sold each year. Fresh from the mold, they gleamed like silver. Most that survive were dredged from the Thames in London. One souvenir rattle in the London Museum once held shells.
